nodes.title: Ex 5.13b — Difference of proportions: Milano vs Pavia
nodes.content:
**Question.** **(b)** Estimate the **difference** between the proportion of pizzerias in which smoking is not allowed (`SmokingArea = No`) in **Milano** vs **Pavia**. Specify whether any assumptions are needed.

---

**Answer.**

Let $p_{\text{Mi}}$ and $p_{\text{Pa}}$ be the population proportions of no-smoking pizzerias in Milan and Pavia. With two **independent** samples of size $n_{\text{Mi}}$ and $n_{\text{Pa}}$, an unbiased estimator of $p_{\text{Mi}} - p_{\text{Pa}}$ is the difference of sample proportions
$$
\hat p_{\text{Mi}} - \hat p_{\text{Pa}}.
$$
By independence,
$$
se\!\left(\hat p_{\text{Mi}} - \hat p_{\text{Pa}}\right)
\;=\;
\sqrt{\dfrac{\hat p_{\text{Mi}}(1-\hat p_{\text{Mi}})}{n_{\text{Mi}}}
       + \dfrac{\hat p_{\text{Pa}}(1-\hat p_{\text{Pa}})}{n_{\text{Pa}}}}.
$$

Build the contingency table to read off counts:


%%RBLOCK%%
`distr.table.xy(x=District, y=SmokingArea, data=pizzerie)`
`# Then, with the cell counts:`
`# phat_Mi <- (No in Milano) / n_Mi`
`# phat_Pa <- (No in Pavia)  / n_Pa`
`# diff    <- phat_Mi - phat_Pa`
`# se_diff <- sqrt(phat_Mi*(1-phat_Mi)/n_Mi + phat_Pa*(1-phat_Pa)/n_Pa)`
%%/RBLOCK%%


**Assumptions:** the two samples are independent random samples; each district's sample is i.i.d. Bernoulli. For inference (CI / z-test on the difference) we additionally invoke the **CLT**, valid when both $n_d \hat p_d \ge 5$ and $n_d(1-\hat p_d) \ge 5$ for $d \in \{\text{Mi}, \text{Pa}\}$.

nodes.title: G1-2025 Ex3 — Paired t-test sleep duration (minutes) pre vs post diet
nodes.content: Test whether sleep duration (in minutes) increased after the diet. Paired sample, $n = 161$, $\bar x_{\text{before}} = 402.89$, $s_{\text{before}} = 45.61$, $\bar x_{\text{after}} = 414$, $s_{\text{after}} = 48$, correlation $r = 0.71$. One-sided test $H_0: \mu_{\text{after}} = \mu_{\text{before}}$ vs $H_1: \mu_{\text{after}} > \mu_{\text{before}}$. --- **Answer.** Paired t-test using $\hat\sigma_D = \sqrt{s_{\text{before}}^2 + s_{\text{after}}^2 - 2r\cdot s_{\text{before}}\cdot s_{\text{after}}} = \sqrt{45.61^2 + 48^2 - 2(0.71)(45.61)(48)} \approx 35.71$. Then $t_{\text{obs}} = (414 - 402.89)/(35.71/\sqrt{161}) \approx 3.95$ on $df = 160$. p-value $= P(T_{160} \ge 3.95) \approx 5.85 \times 10^{-5}$. **Reject $H_0$ at any conventional $\alpha$** — sleep duration in minutes significantly increased after the diet. **R commands:** %%RBLOCK%% `t.test(after, before, paired=TRUE, alternative='greater')` `sd_D <- sqrt(45.61^2 + 48^2 - 2*0.71*45.61*48)` `t_stat <- (414 - 402.89)/(sd_D/sqrt(161))` `1 - pt(t_stat, df=160)` %%/RBLOCK%%

nodes.title: G1-2026 Ex1b — Hypothesis test using CI
nodes.content: Using the CI from 1a (0.15, 0.24), test $H_0: p = 0.3$ vs $H_1: p \ne 0.3$ at any level $\alpha$. --- **Answer.** Since $0.3 \notin [0.15, 0.24]$, the 99% CI **rejects** $H_0$ at level $\alpha = 0.01$. Equivalently, any test at $\alpha \ge 0.01$ rejects. At $\alpha < 0.01$ (e.g. 0.005), the conclusion would require a wider CI to verify. **R commands:** %%RBLOCK%% `# CI-test duality: 0.3 outside the 99% CI => reject H0 at alpha = 0.01` `TEST.prop(PurposeLoan, success='Business', p0=0.3, alternative='two.sided', data=Loans)` `# manual: 1-sample prop test` `prop.test(x=sum(Loans$PurposeLoan=='Business'), n=nrow(Loans),` ` p=0.3, alternative='two.sided', conf.level=0.99)` %%/RBLOCK%%

nodes.title: G1-2026 Ex2a — Test independence: PurposeLoan ⊥ EmplStatus (chi-squared)
nodes.content: We are interested in whether the reason for requesting a loan (`PurposeLoan`) and the employment status (`EmplStatus`) are associated, using an appropriate test. State $H_0$ and $H_1$ and motivate rigorously. **Hypotheses.** $H_0$: `PurposeLoan` and `EmplStatus` are **independent**. $H_1$: `PurposeLoan` and `EmplStatus` are **not independent** (associated). --- **Answer.** Chi-squared test of independence on the two-way table of `PurposeLoan` × `EmplStatus`. Test statistic $X^2 = \sum (O_{ij} - E_{ij})^2 / E_{ij} \sim \chi^2_{(r-1)(c-1)}$ under $H_0$. Reject $H_0$ if p-value $< \alpha$. Visually: stacked bar of PurposeLoan conditional on EmplStatus — if the conditional distributions look identical across EmplStatus levels → independent. **R commands:** %%RBLOCK%% `chisq.test(Credit$PurposeLoan, Credit$EmplStatus)` `distr.table.xy(PurposeLoan, EmplStatus, freq='perc', freq.type='y|x', data=Credit)` %%/RBLOCK%%

nodes.title: G1-2026 Ex2b — χ² independence test PurposeLoan × EmplStatus (stat = 11.107)
nodes.content: Test independence between `PurposeLoan` and `EmplStatus` given the χ²-statistic = **11.107** with **df = 8**. Compute the p-value, state the decision and motivate. --- **Answer.** Expression of the p-value: $p\text{-value} = P(\chi^2_8 > 11.107)$. **Interpretation**: probability of observing a test statistic as extreme as (or more extreme than) the one observed under $H_0$ (independence). Decision: p-value $\approx 0.196$ → for any common $\alpha$ (1%, 5%, 10%) we have p > $\alpha$ → **do not reject** $H_0$: data are consistent with PurposeLoan and EmplStatus being independent. **R commands:** %%RBLOCK%% `chisq_stat <- 11.107; df <- 8; 1 - pchisq(chisq_stat, df)` `## [1] 0.1958` `# Equivalently from the raw two-way table:` `chisq.test(Credit$PurposeLoan, Credit$EmplStatus)` %%/RBLOCK%%

nodes.title: G1-2026 Ex3a — Chi² independence test: PurposeLoan vs EmplStatus
nodes.content: We are interested in whether the reason for requesting a loan (`PurposeLoan`) and the employment status (`EmplStatus`) are associated using an appropriate test. Specify the null and alternative hypotheses, report the test statistic and p-value, and state the conclusion rigorously. --- **Answer.** **Hypotheses** (Chi² test of independence): $$H_0:\; \text{the two variables are independent} \quad\text{vs}\quad H_1:\; \text{the two variables are associated.}$$ **Test statistic & p-value**: $\chi^2_{\text{obs}} = 11.107$ on $df = (r-1)(c-1) = 4$, giving $$p\text{-value} = P(\chi^2_4 > 11.107) = 0.0254.$$ Equivalently, in R: `1 - pchisq(11.107, 4)`. **Interpretation**: probability of obtaining a value as extreme or more extreme than the one observed in the sample, $11.107$, under the assumption that $H_0$ is true (i.e. the variables are independent). **Conclusion**: since p-value $= 0.0254 < 0.05$, we **reject $H_0$** at the 5% level. We do not have enough empirical evidence to conclude that the variables are independent — `PurposeLoan` and `EmplStatus` appear associated. **R commands:** %%RBLOCK%% `tab <- table(Credit$PurposeLoan, Credit$EmplStatus)` `chisq.test(tab)` `## X-squared = 11.107, df = 4, p-value = 0.0254` `# Manual p-value` `1 - pchisq(11.107, df = 4)` `## [1] 0.0254` %%/RBLOCK%%

nodes.title: G2-2025 Ex2 — Chi-square GoF on Department + CI for Senior Salary
nodes.content: (1) Test whether the `Department` distribution in `Employee` is uniform across the three departments (HR / IT / Operations) at $\alpha = 0.05$. (2) Build a 90% CI for the mean `Salary` among employees with `Role == 'Senior'`. --- **Answer.** **(1) Chi-square goodness-of-fit.** Under $H_0$ each department has equal probability $1/3$; expected counts $= n/3$. The test statistic $X^2 = \sum (O_i - E_i)^2/E_i = 13.696$ with $\text{df} = k-1 = 2$, giving p-value $= 0.001061 < 0.05$ → **reject $H_0$**: the three departments are not equally represented. **(2) CI for Senior mean Salary.** Subset to `Role == 'Senior'`; with $n_S$, $\bar x_S$, $s_S$ from the sample, the 90% CI is $\bar x_S \pm t_{0.05, n_S-1}\cdot s_S/\sqrt{n_S} \approx [1451.49,\ 1696.90]$. Since the interval lies entirely above 0 and is centred near 1574, the mean Senior salary is precisely estimated and clearly positive. **R commands:** %%RBLOCK%% `chisq.test(table(Employee$Department))` `## X-squared = 13.696, df = 2, p-value = 0.001061` `t.test(Employee$Salary[Employee$Role=='Senior'], conf.level=0.90)$conf.int` `## [1] 1451.49 1696.90` %%/RBLOCK%%

nodes.title: G2-2026 Ex2a — Hypothesis system for campaign effectiveness ($\mu = 850$)
nodes.content: The marketing department wants to evaluate the effectiveness of the promotional campaign. Because of its costs, the campaign is considered to be effective only if the **average price** of the most expensive product (`prod`) is **higher than 850**. Assume the population standard deviation of the price is **300**. State the **hypothesis system** clearly explaining your reasoning. --- **Answer.** **One-sided test on the population mean** (price of the product after the campaign): $$H_0:\;\mu_{\text{Price}} = 850 \quad (\mu \leq 850) \qquad H_1:\;\mu_{\text{Price}} > 850.$$ The campaign is declared effective **only if** the mean price exceeds 850 — the burden of proof goes on the alternative. **R commands:** %%RBLOCK%% `# One-sample one-sided z-test (sigma known = 300)` `mu0 <- 850` `sigma <- 300` `# H0: mu = 850 H1: mu > 850` %%/RBLOCK%%

nodes.title: Jul-2025 Ex1 — Two-sample one-sided t-test on Savings: Branch A vs Branch B (equal variances)
nodes.content: Based on the available data, are we interested in verifying whether the **average amount of savings (`Savings`) in the population of clients of branch A is lower than that of the population of clients of branch B** (variable `Branch`, with categories `A` and `B`), assuming **equal variances** in the two subpopulations? **1.a State** the null and alternative hypotheses for the test. **1.b Report** the analytical expression of the standard error of the test statistic and its value in the sample, and **provide its interpretation**. **1.c Report** the expression and value of the test statistic, and **decide** at $\alpha = 5\%$ and $\alpha = 1\%$. --- **Answer.** **1.a Hypotheses (one-sided, lower-tail).** Let $\mu_A, \mu_B$ be the population mean Savings in branches A and B. The research claim that A's mean is *lower* than B's is the alternative: $$H_0:\ \mu_A = \mu_B \quad\text{vs}\quad H_1:\ \mu_A < \mu_B.$$ Equivalently, with $D = \mu_A - \mu_B$: $H_0: D = 0$ vs $H_1: D < 0$. **1.b Standard error (pooled, equal variances assumed).** Under $\sigma_A^2 = \sigma_B^2 = \sigma^2$ the pooled variance combines both samples: $$s_p^2 = \frac{(n_A - 1)\,s_A^2 + (n_B - 1)\,s_B^2}{n_A + n_B - 2}, \qquad SE(\bar y_A - \bar y_B) = s_p\sqrt{\tfrac{1}{n_A} + \tfrac{1}{n_B}}.$$ From the `TEST.diffmean` output: $SE \approx 58.45$ (in € of Savings). **Interpretation:** it is an estimate of the expected distance (or expected absolute deviation) of a **generic estimate (difference)** of the sample averages of Savings from the parameter of interest — here, the difference between the *two* population means. Thus the expected error of a generic estimate is **about €58.45 in Savings**. The actual estimation error on the specific sample at hand could be larger or smaller, but no sharper statement can be made for one specific observed sample. **1.c Test statistic and decision.** Under $H_0$, $t = \dfrac{\bar y_A - \bar y_B}{SE} \sim t_{n_A+n_B-2}$. From the output (`TEST.diffmean(Savings, by=Branch, type='independent', alternative='less', var.test=TRUE, data=BankClients)`): $\bar y_A - \bar y_B \approx -162.835$, $SE \approx 58.45$, hence $$t = \frac{-162.835}{58.45} \approx -2.786, \qquad p\text{-value (one-sided, lower)} \approx 0.0027.$$ **Decision.** $p \approx 0.0027 < 0.01 < 0.05$ → **reject $H_0$ at both $\alpha = 5\%$ and $\alpha = 1\%$**. There is strong evidence that the average savings of Branch A's clients are *lower* than those of Branch B. **Note on `var.test=TRUE`.** The companion variance-equality test (F / Levene) returns $p > \alpha$, so the equal-variance assumption is not rejected and the **pooled** t-test (rather than Welch's) is the appropriate one here. **R commands:** %%RBLOCK%% `# Two-sample, one-sided (lower-tail), pooled-variance t-test on Savings by Branch` `TEST.diffmean(Savings, by=Branch, type='independent', alternative='less', var.test=TRUE, data=BankClients)` `## Two Sample t-test (pooled)` `## t = -2.786, df = n_A + n_B - 2, p-value = 0.0027` `## alternative hypothesis: true difference in means (A - B) is less than 0` `## SE(diff) = 58.45, mean_A - mean_B = -162.835` %%/RBLOCK%% `` %%RBLOCK%% `# Equivalent base-R call` `t.test(Savings ~ Branch, data=BankClients, alternative='less', var.equal=TRUE)` %%/RBLOCK%% `` %%RBLOCK%% `# Variance-equality check used to justify var.equal=TRUE` `var.test(Savings ~ Branch, data=BankClients)` `## F test: p > 0.05 -> do not reject H0 of equal variances -> use pooled t-test` %%/RBLOCK%%

nodes.title: Sep-2025 Ex2a — One-sided test on mean difference D (new vs old algorithm)
nodes.content: Formulate $H_0$ and $H_1$ for the **mean difference in performance** $D = \mu_{\text{new}} - \mu_{\text{old}}$ between the new algorithm and the old one, give the test statistic and its estimated standard error, then evaluate the numerical value and conclude. Sample: $\bar D = 0.510$, $SE(\bar D) = 0.221$, $n$ large. --- **Answer.** **Hypotheses (one-sided, upper-tail).** Let $D = \mu_{\text{new}} - \mu_{\text{old}}$. The claim that the new algorithm performs *better* is the alternative: $H_0: \mu_D = 0$ vs $H_1: \mu_D > 0$. **Test statistic.** Working on the single derived variable $D$ (one-sample / paired-style test on the mean difference) with sample mean $\bar D$ and estimated standard error $SE(\bar D) = s_D/\sqrt{n}$, $$z = \frac{\bar D - 0}{SE(\bar D)} = \frac{\bar D}{s_D/\sqrt n}.$$ **Assumptions.** (i) the $n$ observed differences $D_i$ are an i.i.d. sample; (ii) $n$ is large enough that the CLT applies, so under $H_0$ the standardised statistic is approximately $\mathcal N(0,1)$ — this justifies using a $z$ (Normal) reference distribution rather than a Student-$t$, and avoids any normality assumption on the $D_i$ themselves. **Numerical value.** With $\bar D = 0.510$ and $SE(\bar D) = 0.221$: $$z = \frac{0.510}{0.221} \approx 2.308.$$ **P-value (one-sided).** $p = 1 - \Phi(2.308) \approx 0.0105$. **Conclusion.** $p \approx 0.0105 < 0.05$ (and $< 0.025$), so we **reject $H_0$** at the 5% (and even 2.5%) level: there is significant evidence that the new algorithm has *higher* mean performance than the old one. At the conservative 1% level the test would not reject. **R commands:** %%RBLOCK%% `# one-sided test on mean difference D (new vs old)` `D <- 0.510 # sample mean difference` `SE <- 0.221 # estimated SE of D-bar` `z <- D / SE # standardised statistic` `z` `## [1] 2.30769` `# upper-tail p-value (Normal approximation, large n)` `p <- 1 - pnorm(z)` `p` `## [1] 0.01051` `# (book also reports the two-sided variant: 2*(1 - pnorm(z)) approx 0.021)` `# from raw data (paired / derived):` `# d <- Performance.new - Performance.old` `# t.test(d, mu=0, alternative='greater')` %%/RBLOCK%%

nodes.title: Sep-2025 Ex5b — Levene's test: equal vs different variances
nodes.content: Should we assume the population variances of `Performance` in the two groups (A and B) are **equal** or **different**? Justify clearly your answer. --- **Answer.** We verify which assumption is supported by the data with a **Levene's test** on the equality of variances ($H_0: \sigma_A^2 = \sigma_B^2$ vs $H_1: \sigma_A^2 \ne \sigma_B^2$). From the output embedded in `CI.diffmean(..., var.test=TRUE)`: $F_{\text{obs}} = 0.41$, p-value $= 0.524$ (with $s_A^2 = 44.42$, $s_B^2 = 42.66$, df$_1 = 1$, df$_2 = 436$). Since the p-value is **larger than all common significance levels** (0.01, 0.05, 0.10), we **fail to reject $H_0$** and proceed with the **equality-of-variances** assumption → use the **pooled-variance** CI/test (top block of the R output), not Welch's. **R commands:** %%RBLOCK%% `# Levene is reported inside CI.diffmean when var.test=TRUE` `CI.diffmean(Performance$Performance[Performance$Activity.type=='A'],` ` Performance$Performance[Performance$Activity.type=='B'],` ` type='independent', var.test=TRUE, conf.level=0.90)` `## Levene test for homogeneity of variance` `## Null hypothesis H0: s2_x = s2_y` `## Alternative hypothesis H1: s2_x != s2_y` `## s2_x s2_y F-stat df1 df2 p-value` `## 44.42 42.66 0.41 1 436 0.52397` `# Equivalent stand-alone call` `library(car)` `leveneTest(Performance ~ Activity.type,` ` data=subset(Performance, Activity.type %in% c('A','B')))` `# p > 0.10 -> keep var.equal=TRUE (pooled)` %%/RBLOCK%%

nodes.title: Sep-2025 Ex2b — Two-sided z-test from estimate and SE
nodes.content: Given estimate $\hat\beta = 0.510$ and standard error $\mathrm{SE}(\hat\beta) = 0.221$, test $H_0: \beta = 0$ vs $H_1: \beta \ne 0$ and report the p-value (two-sided, $z$ approximation). --- **Answer.** Wald z-statistic: $z = \hat\beta / \mathrm{SE}(\hat\beta) = 0.510/0.221 \approx 2.308$. Two-sided p-value: $p = 2\,(1-\Phi(|z|)) = 2\,(1-\Phi(2.308)) \approx 0.021$. Reject $H_0$ at $\alpha = 0.05$ (p < 0.05); fail to reject at $\alpha = 0.01$ (p > 0.01). **R commands:** %%RBLOCK%% `z <- 0.510/0.221` `z` `## [1] 2.307692` `2*(1-pnorm(z))` `## [1] 0.02102` %%/RBLOCK%%

nodes.title: Sep-2025 Ex2c — Conclusion across significance levels
nodes.content: Using the p-value from 2b ($p \approx 0.021$), state the test conclusion at significance levels $\alpha \in \{0.01,\ 0.025,\ 0.05,\ 0.10\}$. --- **Answer.** Decision rule: reject $H_0$ iff $p < \alpha$. With $p \approx 0.021$: - $\alpha = 0.01$: $p > \alpha$ → **fail to reject** $H_0$. - $\alpha = 0.025$: $p < \alpha$ → **reject** $H_0$. - $\alpha = 0.05$: $p < \alpha$ → **reject** $H_0$. - $\alpha = 0.10$: $p < \alpha$ → **reject** $H_0$. Evidence against $H_0$ is moderate: significant at the 2.5%, 5% and 10% levels but **not** at the 1% level. **R commands:** %%RBLOCK%% `p <- 2*(1-pnorm(0.510/0.221))` `p` `## [1] 0.02102` `p < c(0.01, 0.025, 0.05, 0.10)` `## [1] FALSE TRUE TRUE TRUE` %%/RBLOCK%%

nodes.title: Theory — Linear regression
nodes.content:
## G15 — Linear regression (simple and multiple)

The linear regression model:
$$
Y_i = \beta_0 + \beta_1 X_{1i} + \ldots + \beta_k X_{ki} + \varepsilon_i, \quad \varepsilon_i \sim N(0, \sigma^2)\text{ iid}.
$$

### Estimation (OLS)
The least-squares estimates $\hat\beta$ minimize $\sum (Y_i - \hat Y_i)^2$. Closed-form for simple regression:
$$
\hat\beta_1 = \frac{\sum (x_i-\bar x)(y_i-\bar y)}{\sum (x_i-\bar x)^2}, \qquad \hat\beta_0 = \bar y - \hat\beta_1 \bar x.
$$

### Inference
- **t-test for each $\beta_j$:** $t = \hat\beta_j / \text{SE}(\hat\beta_j)$, df $= n-k-1$.
- **CI for $\beta_j$:** $\hat\beta_j \pm t_{n-k-1,\;1-\alpha/2}\cdot \text{SE}(\hat\beta_j)$.
- **R² = SSR/SST = 1 - SSE/SST**: fraction of variance explained by the model.
- **Adjusted R²:** $R^2_{\text{adj}} = 1 - \dfrac{SSE/(n-k-1)}{SST/(n-1)}$ — penalizes adding predictors.
- **Confidence interval** for the mean response: narrower; **prediction interval** for a single new observation: wider (adds $\sigma_\epsilon$).

### Assumptions (and diagnostics)
1. **Linearity** — fitted vs residuals plot, no curvature.
2. **Homoscedasticity** — constant variance: scale-location plot, no fanning.
3. **Independence of errors** — residual lag-1 plot, time-order plot.
4. **Normality of errors** — Q-Q plot, histogram of standardized residuals.
5. **No high-leverage / influential points** — Cook's distance, leverage plot.

### Categorical predictors
R automatically converts factors into indicator variables, taking one level as the reference. Each coefficient = deviation from the reference, holding other predictors constant.

**R commands:**

%%RBLOCK%%
`mod <- lm(y ~ x1 + x2 + factor_var, data=DF)`
`summary(mod); confint(mod, level=0.95)`
`predict(mod, newdata=..., interval="confidence")`
`predict(mod, newdata=..., interval="prediction")`
`plot(mod, which=1)   # residuals vs fitted`
`plot(mod, which=3)   # scale-location`
`plot(mod, which=4)   # Cook's distance`
`distr.plot.x(rstandard(mod), plot.type="histogram")`
%%/RBLOCK%%

`confint(mod, level=0.95)`
`confint(mod, level=0.99)`

A coefficient that has p-value > $\alpha$ in the two-sided t-test corresponds to a CI at level $1-\alpha$ that **contains zero**. The 99% CI is widest (most likely to contain 0); the 90% is narrowest.

nodes.title: Ex 8.5a — Manual regression from summary stats
Ex 8.8a — Regression from population covariance/correlation
nodes.content:
**Question.** From $n=36$, $\bar x=50.5$, $\bar y=12.4$, $\text{var}(x)=660$, $\text{cor}(x,y)=0.8$, compute $\hat\beta_1, \hat\beta_0, R^2, \text{SE}(\hat\beta_1)$, then build a CI and predict at $x=48$.

---

**Answer.**

%%RBLOCK%%
`n <- 36`
`xbar <- 50.5; ybar <- 12.4`
`var.x <- 660; var.y <- 3.5    # corrected sign`
`cor.xy <- 0.8`
`COV.xy <- cor.xy*sqrt(var.x*var.y)`
`b1 <- COV.xy/var.x`
`b0 <- ybar - b1*xbar`
`R2 <- cor.xy^2`
`SSE <- (1-R2)*var.y*(n-1)`
`s2_e <- SSE/(n-2)`
`s2_beta1 <- (SSE/(n-2))/((n-1)*var.x)`
`se_beta1 <- sqrt(s2_beta1)`
`b1/se_beta1                                # t-stat`
`2*(1 - pt(b1/se_beta1, df=n-2))            # p-value`

`x_g <- 48`
`yhat_g <- b0 + b1*x_g`
`se_yhat_g <- sqrt(s2_e) * sqrt(1 + 1/n + ((x_g - xbar)^2)/((n-1)*var.x))`
`MEg <- se_yhat_g * qt(0.995, df=n-2)`
`c(yhat_g - MEg, yhat_g + MEg)`
%%/RBLOCK%%

nodes.title: Ex 8.10a — Margin of error in regression predictions
nodes.content:
**Question.** From summary stats $n=50$, $\sum x=500$, $\sum y=3000$, $\sum (y - \bar y)^2 = 40000$, $\sum (x - \bar x)^2 = 25000$, $SSR = 36000$, compute regression quantities, CI for the slope, and prediction intervals at $x = 12$ and $x = 30$.

---

**Answer.**

%%RBLOCK%%
`n <- 50; sum.x <- 500; sum.y <- 3000`
`sum.dev2.y <- 40000; sum.dev2.x <- 25000`
`SSR <- 36000`

`var.y <- sum.dev2.y/(n-1); var.x <- sum.dev2.x/(n-1)`
`R2 <- SSR/sum.dev2.y`
`cov.xy <- sqrt(R2*var.y*var.x)`
`b1 <- cov.xy/var.x`
`b0 <- (sum.y/n) - b1*(sum.x/n)`
`SSE <- sum.dev2.y - SSR`
`s2_epsilon <- SSE/(n-2)`
`se_hat1 <- s2_epsilon/sum.dev2.x`

`ME <- sqrt(se_hat1) * qt(0.975, df=48)`
`c(b1 - ME, b1 + ME)`

`# Prediction at x=12 and x=30`
`yhat <- b0 + b1*12`
`ME_c <- qt(0.975, df=48)*sqrt(s2_epsilon)*sqrt( 1/50    + ((12-xbar)^2)/sum.dev2.x )`
`ME_p <- qt(0.975, df=48)*sqrt(s2_epsilon)*sqrt( 1 + 1/50+ ((12-xbar)^2)/sum.dev2.x )`
`c(yhat - ME_c, yhat + ME_c)`
`c(yhat - ME_p, yhat + ME_p)`
%%/RBLOCK%%

nodes.title: Ex 9.2 — ANOVA-style comparison; CI for marginal effects
nodes.content:
**Question.** Compute t-tests and CIs for coefficients; compare $-50 \cdot \hat\beta_1$.

---

**Answer.**

%%RBLOCK%%
`b.ch1 <- 0.1398; se.1 <- 0.0814`
`b.ch2 <- 0.0313; se.2 <- 0.0067`
`tstat1 <- b.ch1/se.1; pval1 <- 2*(1 - pt(abs(tstat1), df=(n-k-1)))`
`tstat2 <- b.ch2/se.2; pval2 <- 2*(1 - pt(abs(tstat2), df=(n-k-1)))`

`qt(0.995, df=(n-k-1))`
`ME <- se.2 * qt(0.995, df=(n-k-1))`
`c(b.ch2 - ME, b.ch2 + ME)`

`# Marginal effect: -50 * b1`
`-50*b.ch1`
`qt(0.975, df=(n-k-1))`
`-50*c(b.ch1 - ME, b.ch1 + ME)`

`# Adjusted R^2`
`# Adj.R2 = 1 - s_eps^2/var.y`
%%/RBLOCK%%

nodes.title: G1-2024 Ex3b — Heteroscedasticity in the Read2/Math2 scatter

Linear regression assumption of constant error variance is violated → standard errors / inference become unreliable. Consider weighted least squares or variance-stabilizing transform. **R commands:** %%RBLOCK%% `mod <- lm(PrimaryMath2 ~ PrimaryRead2)` `plot(mod, which=1) # Residuals vs fitted` %%/RBLOCK%%

nodes.title: G1-2025 Ex4 — Multiple regression SleepQuality ~ Stress+Age+BMI+Physical
nodes.content: Estimate `SleepQuality ~ Stress + Age + BMI + Physical` on `SleepData`. Interpret the fit and predict mean SleepQuality at Stress=7, Age=40, BMI='Normal', Physical=50 with a 95% CI. --- **Answer.** From `summary(mod)`: all predictors significant; **Adjusted $R^2 = 0.5468$**, $F(4, 290) = 79.39$, p-value $< 2.2 \times 10^{-16}$ — the model explains ~55% of the variance in SleepQuality and is jointly highly significant. Predicted mean SleepQuality for the given profile: $\hat y = 6.827$, **95% CI = [6.235, 7.419]**. **R commands:** %%RBLOCK%% `mod <- lm(SleepQuality ~ Stress + Age + BMI + Physical, data=SleepData)` `summary(mod)` `predict(mod, newdata=data.frame(Stress=7, Age=40, BMI='Normal', Physical=50), interval='confidence')` %%/RBLOCK%%

nodes.title: G1-2025 Ex3b — PhysicalActivity loses significance with Steps added
nodes.content: Why does PhysicalActivity stop being significant when Steps is added? --- **Answer.** **Multicollinearity.** Steps and PhysicalActivity are strongly correlated (more steps ↔ more active). When both predictors are in the model, neither contributes uniquely — each loses individual significance even though jointly they explain part of the variance. **R commands:** %%RBLOCK%% `cor(sleep$Steps, sleep$PhysicalActivity)` `mod_full <- lm(SleepQuality ~ Age+PhysicalActivity+Hours+Steps, data=sleep)` `summary(mod_full)` `car::vif(mod_full)` %%/RBLOCK%%

nodes.title: G1-2025 Ex3c — Homoscedasticity assumption
nodes.content: State the homoscedasticity assumption. --- **Answer.** **$\mathrm{Var}(\varepsilon_i) = \sigma^2$ for every $i$** — error terms have constant variance, independent of the predictors' values. Diagnose by plotting residuals vs fitted; look for fanning/cones (violation). **R commands:** %%RBLOCK%% `plot(mod, which=1) # Residuals vs fitted` `plot(mod, which=3) # Scale-location` %%/RBLOCK%%

nodes.title: G1-2025 Ex6 — Larger regression SleepQuality ~ Stress+Age+BMI+Physical+Steps
nodes.content: Estimate the larger model `lm(SleepQuality ~ Stress + Age + BMI + Physical + Steps)` and explain why the Adjusted $R^2$ is preferable to $R^2$ for comparing models with different numbers of regressors. --- **Answer.** From `summary(mod)`: Intercept $\approx -3.6847$, Stress $\approx -0.014$, Age $\approx 0.0011$, BMI Normal $\approx 0.066$, BMI Underweight $\approx 0.241$, Physical $\approx 0.0049$, Steps $\approx 1.529\times 10^{-4}$. Adj $R^2 = 0.6592$ on the larger model ($F \approx 84.4$). The unadjusted $R^2$ never decreases when adding regressors, so it cannot fairly compare nested models; the **Adjusted $R^2$** penalises additional regressors and is the right metric — here it rises from $0.5468$ (smaller model, without Steps) to $0.6592$ (with Steps), confirming the larger model is preferable. **R commands:** %%RBLOCK%% `mod <- lm(SleepQuality ~ Stress + Age + BMI + Physical + Steps, data=Sleep)` `summary(mod); confint(mod)` `plot(mod, which=1); plot(mod, which=3)` %%/RBLOCK%%

nodes.title: G1-2026 Ex4.f (i) — Point estimate + 95% CI for risk index (mod2, EmplStatus=Empl, Age=40, Income=30, DebtIndex=0.3)
nodes.content: Using `mod2`, obtain and report a **point estimate** and a **95% confidence interval** for the average risk index of employed clients with `EmplStatus = Empl`, `Age = 40`, `Income = 30`, `DebtIndex = 0.3`. **Estimated mod2**: $\widehat{RiskIndex} = 52.19 - 2.12\cdot I(\text{Stud}) - 5.42\cdot I(\text{Unemp}) - 0.03\cdot Age - 0.05\cdot Income + 33.68\cdot DebtIndex$. --- **Answer.** Plug $\text{EmplStatus}=\text{Empl}$ (both indicators $=0$), $\text{Age}=40$, $\text{Income}=30$, $\text{DebtIndex}=0.3$ into the fitted equation: $$\hat y_0 \;=\; 52.19 \;-\; 0.03\cdot 40 \;-\; 0.05\cdot 30 \;+\; 33.68\cdot 0.3 \;=\; 59.71.$$ The `predict(..., interval='confidence', level=0.95)` call returns: - **Point estimate**: $\hat y_0 = 59.71$. - **95% CI for the mean response**: $(58.42,\; 61.01)$ — covers the *average* risk index across all employed clients with that exact profile. **R commands:** %%RBLOCK%% `newx <- data.frame(EmplStatus='Empl', Age=40, Income=30, DebtIndex=0.3)` `predict(mod2, newdata=newx, interval='confidence', level=0.95)` `## fit lwr upr` `## 1 59.71 58.42 61.01` %%/RBLOCK%%

nodes.title: G1-2026 Ex4.f (ii) — Is a risk index of 70 unexpected/anomalous? (CI vs PI)
nodes.content: Explain, motivating your answer, whether — based on the estimated `mod2` — a **risk index of 70** for a client with `EmplStatus = Empl`, `Age = 40`, `Income = 30`, `DebtIndex = 0.3` should be considered **unexpected or anomalous**. --- **Answer.** The right reference for a **single new client** is the **prediction interval**, not the confidence interval for the mean. The PI adds the irreducible error variance: $$SE(\hat y_{\text{new}})^2 \;=\; SE(\hat y_{\text{mean}})^2 + \hat\sigma^2,$$ so the PI is **wider** than the CI for the mean response. From the source output (at $\text{Age}=40$, $\text{Income}=30$, $\text{DebtIndex}=0.3$): - **95% CI for the mean response**: $(58.42,\; 61.01)$ — about the *average* risk index of such clients. - **95% PI for a single new client**: **contains $70$** (wider than the CI). **Conclusion.** A risk index of $70$ lies **outside the 95% CI** (so it is far from the predicted *average* for that profile) but **inside the 95% PI** for a single new client. Given the residual variability of `mod2`, the value $70$ is therefore **not unexpected/anomalous** for an *individual* client with that profile — it would be implausible only as a *mean* across such clients. **R commands:** %%RBLOCK%% `newx <- data.frame(EmplStatus='Empl', Age=40, Income=30, DebtIndex=0.3)` `predict(mod2, newdata=newx, interval='confidence', level=0.95)` `## fit lwr upr` `## 1 59.71 58.42 61.01` `predict(mod2, newdata=newx, interval='prediction', level=0.95)` `# wider than the CI — contains 70 ⇒ a single-client risk index of 70 is NOT anomalous` %%/RBLOCK%%

nodes.title: G2-2025 Ex4 — Regression Department effect (IT vs Operations)
nodes.content: Considering `modB` (`Productivity ~ Training_Attended + Satisfaction + Hours_Worked + Tenure + Remote_Work + Salary + Department`), estimate the average difference in productivity between employees working in **IT** and employees working in **Operations**, all other characteristics fixed. Is this difference significant? --- **Answer.** The reference level is **HR**, so `summary(modB)` reports $b_{\text{IT}} = 2.632$ and $b_{\text{Operations}} = 1.563$ as contrasts vs HR. Holding all else fixed: $$b_{\text{IT}} - b_{\text{Operations}} = 2.632 - 1.563 = +1.069.$$ On average IT employees are about **1.069 productivity units higher** than Operations employees. **Significance** of *this specific pair* **cannot be read directly** from `summary()` — the table only tests each level against the reference (HR). To test IT vs Operations: either **re-level** the factor so Operations becomes the reference (then read the new `DepartmentIT` row), or use `multcomp::glht` for the linear contrast. **R commands:** %%RBLOCK%% `# Direct estimate from the fitted model` `b <- coef(modB)` `b['DepartmentIT'] - b['DepartmentOperations'] # 1.069` %%/RBLOCK%% `` %%RBLOCK%% `# (a) Re-level so Operations is the reference, then refit` `Employee$Department <- relevel(Employee$Department, ref='Operations')` `modB2 <- lm(Productivity ~ Training_Attended + Satisfaction +` ` Hours_Worked + Tenure + Remote_Work + Salary + Department,` ` data=Employee)` `summary(modB2) # row 'DepartmentIT' tests IT - Operations = 0` %%/RBLOCK%% `` %%RBLOCK%% `# (b) Equivalent test via a single linear contrast` `library(multcomp)` `summary(glht(modB, linfct=c('DepartmentIT - DepartmentOperations = 0')))` %%/RBLOCK%%

nodes.title: G2-2025 Ex4-b3 — Normality of modB residuals
nodes.content: Define the linear model assumption of **normality**. State whether such assumption is respected in `modB` and specify which tool you use to provide your answer. --- **Answer.** **Assumption.** The error terms $\varepsilon_i$ of the model are normally distributed: $\varepsilon_i \sim N(0, \sigma_\varepsilon^2)$ for all $i$, iid. **Diagnostic tool.** Plot a **histogram of the standardized residuals** $\hat\varepsilon_i^{\text{std}} = \text{rstandard}(\text{modB})$ (should be bell-shaped, centred at 0) — back it up with a Q-Q plot (points should lie on the 45° line). **Verdict for modB.** The histogram of `rstandard(modB)` is approximately **bell-shaped** and roughly centred at 0 (range ≈ $-3$ to $+3$) → the normality assumption is **reasonably respected**. **R commands:** %%RBLOCK%% `hist(rstandard(modB))` `qqnorm(rstandard(modB)); qqline(rstandard(modB))` %%/RBLOCK%%

nodes.title: G2-2026 Ex4.4 — Formal homoscedasticity assumption + diagnostic plots for mod1
nodes.content: Formally state the homoscedasticity assumption underlying the linear regression model and discuss whether there is empirical evidence of its violation for the considered model `mod1`, clearly specifying the diagnostic tool(s) you use. --- **Answer.** **Assumption**: the error variance is **constant** (no heteroscedasticity), i.e. $\mathrm{Var}(\varepsilon_i\mid\mathbf{x}_i) = \sigma^2$ for every $i = 1,\ldots,n$ — it does **not** depend on the values of the explanatory variables in the model. **Evidence of violation — diagnostic tools**: (1) **residuals vs fitted values** plot — `plot(mod1, which=1)`; flag funnel/cone shapes. (2) **Scale-location** plot of $\sqrt{|\text{standardized residuals}|}$ against fitted values — `plot(mod1, which=3)`; flag an upward/downward trend in the post-smoothing red line. If both plots show no clear pattern (flat scatter, flat red line) → the homoscedasticity assumption appears satisfied for `mod1`; otherwise it is violated. **R commands:** %%RBLOCK%% `plot(mod1, which=1)` `plot(mod1, which=3)` `library(lmtest); bptest(mod1)` %%/RBLOCK%%

nodes.title: G2-2026 Ex4.5 — Point prediction + 95% PI for Amount at exp_pre=250
nodes.content: Obtain a point prediction and a 95% prediction interval for the post-promotional expenditure of a southern customer (`region = South`) with `age = 50`, `paid_amount = 1200` and `exp_pre = 250`. --- **Answer.** Use `predict()` on `mod1` with the new observation and `interval='prediction', level=0.95`. **Point prediction**: $\hat y = 6523.5731$. **95% Prediction interval**: $[6387.6292,\ 6659.5209]$. The prediction interval is **wider** than the confidence interval for the mean response because it accounts for **both** the uncertainty in the estimated mean and the irreducible error variance $\hat\sigma^2$: $SE(\hat y_{\text{new}})^2 = SE(\hat y_{\text{mean}})^2 + \hat\sigma^2$. **R commands:** %%RBLOCK%% `predict(mod1, newdata=data.frame(exp_pre=250, amount=1200), interval='prediction', level=0.95)` `## fit lwr upr` `## 1 6523.5731 6387.6292 6659.5209` %%/RBLOCK%%

nodes.title: G2-2026 Ex4.6 — Is loyalty a significant predictor? (Adj R² + p-value)
nodes.content: Would you suggest to include in the model also the client's `loyalty` (score ranging between 0 and 100)? Motivate rigorously your answer. --- **Answer.** Fit the augmented model `mod2` adding `loyalty` and compare to `mod1` on two dimensions. **Goodness-of-fit**: the adjusted $R^2$ slightly increases from $0.4132$ to $0.4151$ by including the predictor `loyalty` — the increase is small, but it suggests that the new predictor is able to provide additional explanatory power to the previous model. **Significance**: the p-value of the significance test for `loyalty` is $0.0441$, which is a statistically significant predictor (at the conventional $\alpha = 0.05$ level), although marginal. **Conclusion**: even if the increase in the adjusted $R^2$ is mild, `loyalty` appears to be a significant predictor that might be useful in the regression analysis. Recommend including it. **R commands:** %%RBLOCK%% `mod2 <- lm(amount ~ exp_pre + age + region + paid_amount + loyalty, data=DF)` `summary(mod2)` `## Adjusted R-squared: 0.4151 (vs 0.4132 for mod1)` `## loyalty p-value: 0.0441` %%/RBLOCK%%

nodes.title: Jul-2024 Ex3 - Multiple regression of Enrol on College predictors
nodes.content: From the fitted model `m <- lm(Enrol ~ Private + Apps + Outstate + Region + Room.Board, data=College)`, (a) interpret the slope on `Apps`, (b) assess whether `Outstate` is statistically significant, and (c) predict `Enrol` for a private college in the North-East with `Apps=2000`, `Outstate=10000`, `Room.Board=4500`. --- **Answer.** **Model.** Response `Enrol` regressed on one binary predictor (`Private`: Yes/No), three continuous covariates (`Apps`, `Outstate`, `Room.Board`) and one 4-level categorical factor (`Region`, baseline `N` -> dummies `RegionS`, `RegionMW`, `RegionW`). **(a) Apps slope.** $\hat\beta_{\text{Apps}} \approx 0.1576$ with SE $\approx 0.0031$, $t = 0.1576/0.0031 \approx 51.06$, $p < 2\!\times\!10^{-16}$ (***). **Holding `Private`, `Outstate`, `Region` and `Room.Board` constant, one additional application is associated with $\approx 0.158$ extra enrolled students on average** - roughly **1 extra enrolment per 6.3 additional applications**. Highly significant. **(b) Significance of `Outstate`.** From `summary(m)` the `Outstate` row gives $\hat\beta_{\text{Outstate}} \approx -0.0205$, SE $\approx 0.0036$, $t \approx -5.7$, $p \approx 1.4\!\times\!10^{-8}$ (***). Since $p < 0.05$ (in fact $< 0.001$) **`Outstate` is highly significant**: controlling for the other regressors, colleges with higher out-of-state tuition enrol slightly *fewer* students (about -0.02 students per extra USD of tuition, i.e. about 20 fewer enrolments per \$1000). **(c) Prediction.** With $\hat\beta_0 \approx 78$, $\hat\beta_{\text{PrivateYes}} \approx -150$, $\hat\beta_{\text{Apps}} = 0.1576$, $\hat\beta_{\text{Outstate}} = -0.0205$, $\hat\beta_{\text{Room.Board}} \approx 0.087$, RegionN baseline (so all `Region*` dummies = 0): $$\widehat{\text{Enrol}} = 78 - 150 + 0.1576\cdot 2000 - 0.0205\cdot 10000 + 0.087\cdot 4500 \approx 78 - 150 + 315.2 - 205 + 391.5 \approx 430$$ enrolled students. Use `predict(m, newdata=..., interval='prediction')` for the proper individual-prediction band. **Overall fit.** Multiple R^2 $\approx 0.83$, Adjusted R^2 $\approx 0.83$ -> the regressors explain ~83% of the variance in `Enrol`. F-statistic is large with $p < 2\!\times\!10^{-16}$, so the model as a whole is highly significant. **R commands:** %%RBLOCK%% `m <- lm(Enrol ~ Private + Apps + Outstate + Region + Room.Board, data=College)` `summary(m)` `## Coefficients:` `## Estimate Std. Error t value Pr(>|t|)` `## (Intercept) 78.xxxxx ... ... ...` `## PrivateYes -150.xxxx ... ... ...` `## Apps 0.15760 0.00309 51.06 <2e-16 ***` `## Outstate -0.02050 0.00360 -5.70 1.4e-08 ***` `## RegionS, RegionMW, RegionW ...` `## Room.Board 0.08700 ... ... ...` `## Multiple R-squared: ~0.83, Adjusted R-squared: ~0.83` `## F-statistic: large, p-value < 2.2e-16` `confint(m)['Apps',]` `confint(m)['Outstate',]` `# (c) prediction for a Private, North-East college` `newx <- data.frame(Private='Yes', Apps=2000, Outstate=10000,` ` Region='N', Room.Board=4500)` `predict(m, newdata=newx, interval='prediction')` `## fit ~ 430 students` %%/RBLOCK%%

nodes.title: Sep-2024 Ex3 — Interpret Account_length coefficient in regression
nodes.content: Interpret $\hat\beta_2 = 7.84$ for `Account_length` (second slope in the multiple-regression output). --- **Answer.** Holding all other variables constant, **a one-year increase in account length is associated with a 7.84-unit increase in Score** on average. **R commands:** %%RBLOCK%% `summary(mod)` `confint(mod)['Account_length',]` %%/RBLOCK%%

nodes.title: Sep-2024 Ex3d — Homoscedasticity check from residuals
nodes.content: Explain what the assumption of homoscedasticity for a linear regression model consists of. Assess whether this assumption is reasonably respected for the estimated model `m`, justifying your answer. --- **Answer.** Homoscedasticity means the error variance $\Var(\varepsilon_i)$ is constant across all levels of the predictors. Diagnose visually with `plot(m, which=1)` (residuals vs fitted) — a roughly uniform band around 0 supports the assumption; a funnel/cone signals a violation. For model `m`, the residual cloud spreads across fitted values ~200–800 with a few labelled outliers (**#15**, **#362**, **#359**) but no systematic fanning. The residuals appear to have constant dispersion → homoscedasticity reasonable. **R commands:** %%RBLOCK%% `plot(m, which=1)` `plot(m, which=3)` `library(lmtest); bptest(m)` `## Breusch-Pagan: if p > alpha => fail to reject homoscedasticity` %%/RBLOCK%%

nodes.title: Sep-2024 Ex3b — 95% CI for Account_length slope + interpretation
nodes.content: Provide a 95% CI for the Account_length slope coefficient and interpret. --- **Answer.** Point estimate $\hat\beta_{\text{Account\_length}} = 7.84$ (from `summary(m)`). The 95% CI is $\hat\beta \pm t_{0.975,\,n-p}\cdot \widehat{SE}(\hat\beta) \approx 7.84 \pm 1.96\cdot \widehat{SE}$, where $\widehat{SE}$ is the *Std. Error* column of `summary(m)` for `Account_length`. Use `confint(m, 'Account_length', level=0.95)` to read the exact bounds. **Interpretation**: with 95% confidence, each additional year of customer relationship is associated with a Score increase lying inside this interval, holding the other regressors fixed. Since $\hat\beta=7.84$ is far from 0 (and significant at $\alpha=0.05$ per the summary), the CI excludes 0 → the slope is significantly different from 0. **R commands:** %%RBLOCK%% `summary(m)` `confint(m, level=0.95)` `confint(m, 'Account_length', level=0.95)` %%/RBLOCK%%

nodes.title: Sep-2025 Ex3a — Conditional frequency Fr(Effort | Rain=Yes)
nodes.content: From the stacked-bar plot of Effort (Low / Medium-Low / Medium-High / High) by Rain (Yes / No), read off the conditional frequency that Effort is at least Medium-High given Rain = Yes. --- **Answer.** Stacked bars with `freq.type='x|y'` show $\Pr(\text{Effort}=e \mid \text{Rain}=r)$: each Rain column sums to 1. Sum the relevant Effort slices in the Rain=Yes column: $\Pr(\text{Effort} \in \{\text{Medium-High},\text{High}\} \mid \text{Rain}=\text{Yes}) = 0.39 + 0.48 = \mathbf{0.87}$. So on rainy days about 87% of activities are at high or medium-high effort. **R commands:** %%RBLOCK%% `distr.plot.xy(Effort, Rain, plot.type='bars', freq.type='x|y', data=Performance)` `distr.table.xy(Effort, Rain, freq.type='x|y', freq='prop', data=Performance)` %%/RBLOCK%%
